speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 113, to amend the criminal code.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been asked to give a brief explanation of the proposed bill. For the information of hon. mem-
Criminal Code

bers may I say that the bill consists largely of amendments to clauses which now appear in the criminal code. There are one or two new clauses, however, of which the first and most important is an enactment to punish what might be called nude parades or processions which sometimes take place in some of the western parts of the Dominion of Canada, and which have caused a great deal of trouble in the provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia. The present clause dealing with indecent exposure is not strong enough to prevent such parades and requests have come from the authorities in the western provinces asking that a new section be passed. The proposed penalty for taking part in nude parades will be up to three years' imprisonment.
The next section to which I shall refer prohibits the use of living bacilli as rat poison. The use of such bacilli is very dangerous and the Department of Public Health have asked that such use be prohibited.
The question of chicken stealing is one in regard to which the department has had a great many communications from all parts of Canada. I refer more particularly to the wholesale theft of poultry where organized gangs go out and clean out a poultry house in a few minutes. The penalty at present imposed is very slight and magistrates have taken a very lenient view of such thefts. The proposal is to increase the penalties.
The next change relates to the publication of false advertisements. Retail merchants' associations and better business associations have asked for the change, and there is a special clause protecting newspapers which in good faith publish such advertisements.
The next section provides for the adoption of Bill No. 34 on the order paper concerning the use of counterfeit seals, and applies chiefly to the liquor trade. This provision has been asked for by all the provincial governments with the exception of one, and by the liquor control boards of the various provinces. The section following concerns the same matter and is asked for by the Ontario Liquor Control Board whose seals in a great many instances have been forged.
The next section relates to the selling of goods falsely marked, and is placed in the act at the request of retail merchant associations throughout Canada.
Section 10 merely provides for the repeal of the section now in the criminal code in regard to the soliciting and carrying on of the insurance business. The section now in the code has been pronounced ultra vires by the

judicial committee of the privy council and the present change merely provides for the removal of that section.
Section 11 deals with false fire alarms. In some of the larger cities of Canada the practice of sending in false alarms has become prevalent. It is proposed to provide penalties for those sending in such alarms.
There is an amendment to the section in regard to injuries to animals.
The next amendment concerns appeals to the supreme court from the courts of appeal in the various provinces where there has been a difference of opinion in the appellate courts of those provinces.
Section 15 adopts Bill No. 46 now appearing on the order paper concerning bail in cases under appeal.
I think there is another slight amendment to section 1025 which I seem to have omitted from the draft bill but which I shall ask the committee to insert when the bill reaches the committee stage.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Before this motion carries
I should like to take a few moments to direct the attention of the house, and particularly of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Murphy), to a grievance of rather long standing. I have taken up this matter with the Department of Indian Affairs and have been unable to get any satisfactory statement from them; hence the only course open to me is to bring the matter to the attention of the house. Being our wards, the Indians are without other recourse than an appeal to parliament. I for one have been always of the opinion that the government of Canada has sought to deal fairly with the Indians, and I should like to think that this position is maintained even in matters that may be considered by us of minor importance. It may be because I have been in the west for nearly fifty years that the Indians wrote me with regard to this matter. The unsatisfactory replies of the department led me to inquire more particularly into this case. With reference to a certain lease to the Antapa club covering a portion of the Pasqua Indian reservation, I asked the department:
Will said lease permit the members of the Antapa club to take liquor on to the Indian reservation?
The answer I received, on May 4, was "No." A letter from the department under date of April 23 went further and said:
fMr. Neill.I
The lease to the Antapa shooting club does not permit the members to bring liquor into that portion of the reserve under lease, in fact the lease contains a provision directly to the contrary.
Yet clause 6 of the lease reads:
It is further agreed that the lessee shall not nor will sell or permit or suffer to be sold on the said premises any spirituous liquors, ale, beer, or any intoxicating liquors whatever, except ....
Let me repeat that word:
.... except to members of the said club.
That is, the liquor is permitted to be taken to the premises of the club, which is contrary to the Indian Act and also, I believe, a breach of the Saskatchewan liquor act. That, I would say, is the first misrepresentation of the department. Then the department replied to a question of mine:
The letter which you have received and which purports-
Purports:
-to be signed by the chief of the Pasqua band is almost identical with one or two communications addressed to the department by Mr. Galwey-Foley.
This statement is made notwithstanding the repeated protests of the Indians; in fact, I am informed that a delegation of Indians actually came down here, so evidently an effort is being made by the department to side-step any inquiry. According to the department the whole difficulty is attributable to the interference of a troublesome white man. The letter proceeds:
This lease to the Antapa shooting club has given the department a great deal of trouble, which I am convinced has in the main been caused by the interference of persons resident in that district but not members of the band. In this connection I would mention particularly a gentleman by the name of P. N. B. Galwey-Foley, a white man, who I understand now lives at what is known as Leader's Point adjoining the Pasqua reserve.
I have yet to learn that it is a crime to be a white man, or to protest against injustices on the part of official white men towards the Indians. I do not know anything personally about this Mr. Galwey-Foley except that according to the correspondence brought down I note that he is an ex-imperial officer. Further, to use his own words:
With regard to my integrity, I have the honour to suggest the name of Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor of Montreal.
Yet the department apparently takes the view that he is just poor white trash who can be disregarded.

What is the date of
that lease?

Pasqua Indian Reservation

I shall come to that in a few moments. Mr. Galwey-Foley wrote to the Hon. Charles Stewart under date January 4, 1930, as follows:
It is possible that you are unaware that prior to negotiations being opened for the lease in question it was customary for Commissioner Graham to furnish permits to his friends to shoot on the Pasqua reservation irrespective of the wishes of the Indians notwithstanding the fact that the number of persons supplied with these permits in many instances prohibited the Indians 'from availing themselves of shooting ducks on their reservation for their own immediate needs and I might further state that in the great majority of such eases the Indians received no compensation from those taking advantage of such permits. This state of affairs was in vogue for a number of years prior to application for a lease of the Antapa point being applied for and in my humble opinion constituted a very justifiable grievance from which however the Indians were unable to obtain any redress from the commissioner, notwithstanding their frequent protests; this phase of the situation continued up until the close of the shooting season just passed.
Now, some years ago there was an application from a Mr. McDonald for a lease and it was refused on the ground that it was for a millionaire of New York. Commissioner Graham, in a letter to the department dated August 27, 1926, stated that he had received an application from Mr. McDonald for a lease, and attached to this letter was a copy of one which Commissioner Graham had received from Indian Agent Dodd, intimating that Mr. McDonald wished to obtain the lease for a prominent millionaire of New York, a Mr. Bernard M. Baruch. A similar statement was made to the present Prime Minister by the former Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) on May 20, 1929. I quote:
The present disagreement was brought about a year and a half ago by Mr. D. H. McDonald of Fort Qu'Appelle who without the knowledge or consent of the department held a meeting of the Indians and secured their consent to a lease of this point for. as we were subsequently informed, certain wealthy Americans including Mr. Bernard Baruch of New York.
It was considered by the department that reputable and responsible citizens of this country should receive first consideration.

Canada
first.

Yes; reputable and responsible citizens of this country should receive first consideration. But I am sure my hon. friend does not want us to be deluded by t'he Canada first cry into doing a substantial injustice. Mr. McDonald is now deceased; but in the return I find this statement from him to the acting deputy superintendent general, Vancouver, September 9, 1927:
The statements that I am acting for United States citizens are untrue and evidently made to prejudice my lease. If necessary the department can confine shooting privileges in my lease to British subjects. I challenge the statements referred to in your letter. . .
I am a bona fide citizen and lifelong resident in province, and have complied with requirements of Indian Act in connection with lease.
The above telegram was confirmed and amplified in a subsequent letter, and I have no doubt that this gentleman was telling the truth. He definitely denies that he was acting for anyone in the United States, and he declares that if there is any doubt about it he is willing to have the shooting privileges given to bona fide citizens. The lease to him was rejected on this flimsy ground, and I should not mind it so much were it not that this misrepresentation is continually repeated. When I tried to get the letters from the department there was apparently a desire to withhold some of them from the return.
The department next invokes property rights and in a statement to me says:
For a number of years this club has owned and occupied a property on Dominion lands directly across from Antapa point, which is Indian land. Before the issue of this lease the members of this club, during a few days in each season enjoyed shooting privileges on this point and for these privileges were always fairly generous in their treatment of the individual Indians. As a matter of fact Antapa point is so located that had the shooting rights thereon been granted to other parties, the value of the club property for this purpose would have been completely destroyed, as the flight of the ducks from the marsh to the lake is directly over the point.
But let me point out that the property rights, so-called, were acquired after the negotiations. The final negotiations for the property referred to were completed only in the year 1927, when the five acres of land mentioned were purchased for the club from a local farmer. This was during the period when the late Mr. D. H. McDonald's application was under consideration. With regard to Mr. Graham's part in this matter, I wrote to the department:
It would seem to me that Mr. Graham could not in propriety occupy the dual position of being a member of the Antapa club and also the official responsible for the protection of the rights of the wards of the government.
To this the department made no reply.
It was then that I asked for that correspondence, and this gives still further ground for dissatisfaction. According to it it seems to me that Commissioner Graham cuts a sorry figure. I have read Mr. Galwey-Foley's charge of favouritism. Mr. Graham's letter to Mr. Scott, of January 14, 1928, with regard to one of his officials, says:



Pasqxut Indian Reservation
I may say I find fault with the agent for not first taking the matter up with the department either through this office or direct.
Apparently he is willing to let down one of his officials. Then Commissioner Graham, in a communication dated October 29, 1929, defending himself, states:
The two permits which I did issue were to friends from Winnipeg who were out shooting. ... I would ask the department to let this matter rest in my hands, and to notify the chief, through the agent, that they understand the situation and that the matter should be left in the hands of the agent and myself, to do as we think best. If they are given to understand definitely that it is in the hands of the department, it might make them a little more satisfied.
Here is the commissioner, himself interested in getting the permit, asking the department to leave the whole matter in his hands, and saying that if it is left in his hands the Indians, in his opinion, will be more satisfied. This is a rather interesting attitude for a public official.
Next comes a memorandum from Mr. J. C. Caldwell, director of the lands and timber branch of the Department of Indian Affairs to the deputy superintendent general, with an annotation, "I agree." This annotation, I presume, is from the deputy minister-the initials are D. C.S. The letter states:
I am compelled to state that I do not think the situation is clearly set forth in Mr. Graham's letter. There is no doubt whatever but that someone gave permission or permits to a considerable number of outsiders to shoot on Leader's point and this the Indians of the reserve very keenly resent. ... As Antapa point is now under lease to the Antapa Shooting Club of Regina, Leader's point is the only remaining shooting ground for the Indians and I do not think that any shooting privileges should be granted there other than that approved by the Indians themselves and given to Sir Frederick Haultain. I would suggest that Commissioner Graham be informed that such is the decision of the department and unless he is in a position to submit some very strong argument in opposition to also tell him that we propose informing Chief Pasqua to this effect.
Here we have the deputy minister taking the commissioner to task because of misrepresentations he has made to the department. Mr. Graham appears to be obedient but he is somewhat sulky. He writes to Mr. Scott, on November 16, 1929, as follows:
I shall see that your instructions are carried out to the letter, although I feel that we are now paving the way for a great deal of trouble for the agent and myself. I am disappointed that my way of handling the situation has not met with your approval. I note it is your intention to write direct to the chief, and I would point out that whatever letter you do write to the Indians will be passed round to the outside public, including the gentlemen I 
have referred to, and I would ask the department not to place me in an embarrassing position with the Indians by making it appear that I was in the wrong, as I still think I was handling the situation in the best interest of the Indians.
Here is an official who says that it must not be made to appear to the Indians that he is in the wrong. This man is himself a member of the club which receives the benefits which are in dispute.
Now we come to the lease itself.- I will not take up the time of the house by reading in full the charges made by the chief. He states that the lease was granted not only without their consent but practically against their wishes and in contravention of the treaty act. This lease was granted to a syndicate known the the Antapa Shooting Club of Regina Limited, of which club Indian Commissioner W. M. Graham is a member. The chief complains that methods bordering on coercion were adopted for the purpose of endeavouring to force his tribe to surrender what they regard as their rights as contained in section 51 of the Indian Treaty Act. The chief states:

and we have not to date received any compensation for loss of rental amounting to SI,150 which we were deprived of owing to the department refusing to sanction the lease which was far more advantageous to us and had been unanimously approved by my people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman refer to the terms of the lease itself?

I will come to that in a moment. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) had some knowledge of this matter, as has the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart), who was formerly the minister in charge of this department.
Make it snappy.

I am hurrying as quickly as I can. The history of the lease is briefly as follows:
In 1924 the Antapa club of Regina offered the Indians $150 per year for certain privileges. A lease was made out in 1925, which lease was returned. The reason is given. Under date of January 19, 1925, Mr. D. C. Scott wrote to Mr. W. M. Graham, as follows:
The agreement which accompanied this communication is returned herewith as it is of no use. It is not a properly executed agreement, neither is it a surrender from the band. If the enclosed surrender is approved by the Pasqua band upon return of the documents completed and attested, the question of lease will then receive consideration.

Pasqua Indian Reservation
At that time the Antapa club had no rights which were recognized; it had simply made an application and had offered a form of lease which was not in fact a lease. In 1926 Mr. McDonald made an application for a lease and offered $550 per year payable in advance. This is shown in the letter of the hon. member for West Edmonton to the present Prime Minister dated May 20, 1929. This letter gave a history of the case and stated that Indian Agent Geo. S. Dodd had been present at the meeting of the Indians, who were unanimously in favour of the lease to Mr. McDonald on the terms offered. Mr. Dodd explained at that time that the lease would be subject to the approval of the department. So far everything seemed to be in order. But other influences were at work. The following is a memorandum of Mr. D. C. Scott, dated September 29, 1926:
The Antapa Shooting Club in their application suggested an annual rental of $150 for the privileges involved, which sum in itself would appear sufficient but as the Indians have now signed an agreement and have been promised an annual rental of $550, the matter is, as you will see, very much complicated.
I should think it would be rather complicated. This club had as a member the Indian commissioner. An offer had been made by another party to pay a rental of $550 per year in advance, and that offer had to be side-tracked. It was stated that the offer was made by a New York millionaire, but we have the statement of Mr. McDonald, a former member of the provincial house, now deceased, to the effect that he was not asking for any but Canadian citizens. The following is a letter dated November 23, 1926, from Mr. D. C. Scott to Mr. E. B. Jonah, who was acting for the Antapa club:
It will be necessary for your club to obtain the consent of a majority of the voting members of the Pasqua band before the department could give favourable consideration to your application. A copy of the agreement which Mr. McDonald made with the Pasqua band is enclosed herewith, and I may add that it bears the signatures of a majority of the voting members of the band. It appears that the Pasqua band is opposed to granting any formal release or surrender of this portion of the reserve for the purpose indicated, but if you succeed in obtaining the signatures of a majority of the voting members to a similar agreement, the department is prepared to agree to the terms and conditions set forth in your letter, but of course these terms and conditions must be approved by the band before any further action can be taken.
That was the attitude of Mr. Scott in 1926, an attitude perfectly correct and I believe in harmony with the Indian Act. The signatures for the consent of the band have never been
22110-234 J
obtained and yet a lease has been granted under date of January 14, 192S. The hon. member for West Edmonton wrote to the present Prime Minister under date of May 20, 1929, as follows:
It is the practice of the department whenever possible and within reason to act in accordance with the wishes of the members of the band, but in this case it was felt that in the general interest an exception should be made.
The hon. member practically states that it is the practice of the department to act in accordance with the law when it suits the department. The minister was there to carry out the terms of the Indian Act, but he puts it aside on the ground that this exception is in the general interest. How is it in the general interest? It was in the interest of Mr. Graham and other members of the Antapa club, but it was not in the interest of Mr. McDonald who stated that he was willing that the lease should be made out in such a form as to permit only British subjects to shoot in that territory. Cancellation was refused and Mr. D. C. Scott wrote to Chief Ben Pasqua, under date of February 16, 1931, as follows:
It has been decided that this lease is of decided advantage to your band and sufficient reason has not at any time been advanced which, in our estimation, would justify cancellation.
Apparently the department has reviewed the situation and has refused to cancel the lease which contains clauses opposed to the Indian Act, especially with reference to the importation of liquor into the reserve. This lease was granted after refusal of the application of another Canadian who had offered more advantageous terms. This action was taken after the department had definitely set aside the act under which it is stipulated that the consent of the majority of the Indians must be obtained before a lease can be granted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to indicate the term of the lease? I recall looking into the matter, and I thought the provision with respect to the term of the lease, as compared with the usual lease, was very much in favour of the Indians. Would he look at it?
I have the lease under my hand. I am not suggesting that on its face it is not a favourable lease.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As to the length of time.

The length of time is longer than might be expected and they get this money regularly. I would point out

Pasqua Indian Reservation
however that the club had to pay S550 instead of $150 because of the other offer that was made the Indians by Mr. McDonald.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am relying only on memory, but am I not right in saying that instead of its being a lease of the land within the Indian Act, it is merely a lease of the right to shoot? I remember when I investigated the matter I became impressed with that fact.

I know the Prime Minister, when in opposition, made some inquiries, and I think, if I may say so, he was somewhat misled by the department, as I was misled by the letters which I received. It was not until I looked into the correspondence that I felt that the department had not been playing fair. That is my only reason for having taken the matter up in the house As a layman I am not prepared to say just when a lease is not a lease, but I would point out to the Prime Minister that the lease itself is in this form:
By these presents doth demise and lease unto the said party of the second part. . . . and the lessee has hereunto affixed its seal.
And so on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What did they lease- the land or the right to shoot?
The right to shoot.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what I thought.

This is the point: In the earlier negotiations the department had clearly recognized the necessity of obtaining the consent of the band. The document is constantly spoken of as a lease and in the earlier correspondence it is shown that the department insisted that the consent of the majority of the members of the band should be obtained. May I say further in reply to the Prime Minister: although I am not a lawyer, I believe a recent decision in the courts of Saskatchewan would seem to indicate that I am correct in suggesting that this bind of document is a real lease as contemplated by the Indian Act.
I would charge this: that there has been a series of misrepresentations by the department; that Commissioner Graham, a member of the Antapa club, through misrepresentation, managed to secure the refusal of the lease to one party, and to secure the lease for the club of which he was a member. I think that is a matter which requires departmental action. I know this cannot be settled to-day, but I have taken this occasion to lay it before the house, and I think the minister would be well advised to consider the state-

memt that his own commissioner, a public official, who is a member of the club, has managed to secure these privileges through misrepresentation of the general situation.
I have already pointed out that the clause with regard to liquor violates the terms of the Indian Act, a copy of which I have under my hand and which I can read if necessary. The lease is illegal as being granted without the consent of the band and undoubtedly the whole transaction constitutes a grievance which the Indians feel deeply.
That after all is the most important consideration that I could bring before the house, namely, that the whole manner of handling the situation constitutes in the minds of the Indians a very serious grievance. I know some members may say: They are only a few Indians; who cares? It may further be pointed out that some of the members of the club are quite respectable citizens of the city of Regina, I am given to understand that some of them do not know just the representations that were made in order that the lease could be secured1; indeed I can hardly understand that any respectable citizen would want to take advantage of people who are, after all, wards of the government. I ask for a thorough inquiry on the part of the department, and since the present minister has had nothing whatever to do with the past, I would urge that he consider the question of the cancellation of the lease which, I believe, has not been obtained by a method that would justify itself to the members of the house and to the country at large.

As my name appears very prominently in the observations made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with regard to this lease, although I can speak only from memory and one does not want to depend too greatly upon one's memory respecting a multitude of actions of this kind-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hope not of this kind.

If my hon. friend will read the Indian Act he will find that the department and the minister have full authority to deal with matters that are in dispute so far as the Indians are concerned. It is quite true the department invariably tries to secure the consent of the Indians, but that is not always possible, more particularly, may I say, when people get into a dispute in regard to certain privileges that are being granted upon these reserves. That was the case in the instance mentioned by my hon. friend. It ran over a period of some two or

three years. The application was on behalf of a group of New Yorkers who desired to secure this privilege as against a group of gentlemen in Regina, some of them on the bench, and all, so far as I know, gentlemen of good repute. When the department was finally called upon to make a decision, it gave the lease at the same rental to the Canadian citizens living in Regina.

Does the hon.
member mean to sweep aside this declaration by Mr. McDonald?

Mr. Mc-
Donald, when he found he could not secure a lease for the New Yorkers, later made an application for himself. I did not pay much attention to that. His first application, as is very clear from the evidence the hon. member has himself given to the house, was on behalf of a group of New Yorkers. Subsequently when he found that was to be refused, he made application for himself, but in the meantime, the Regina club was quite willing to accept a lease and pay the rental that was asked. I am not going to say that I would change my opinion one iota with respect to the granting of this lease. If my hon. friend will study the Indian Act, he will find full authority for every action taken by the department. As regards taking liquor on the reserve, the law is very clear and all that has to be done is to institute prosecution. It is an infraction of the law.
It is permitted by the lease.

It is not
permitted by the lease. That is all I have to say in connection with the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I understand it, the
laid down price, including freight c.i.f. Montreal is 3|. This item has engaged the attention of the department for a good deal of time. Last fall a change was made in the rate that had theretofore existed. This practically restores the rate in force prior to September. There is a treaty outstanding with Norway, and representations were made by the consul general of that kingdom with respect to the matter, and we also received representations with respect to the industry in Great Britain. In view of the facilities for export provided for by our packers, one in particular, that sells the product in thirty countries, it was felt, having regard to the representations made last fall, which on investigation were found to be strictly accurate, that this item should be restored to its former position.

This item previous to
September last was under a specific duty and all products of this kind coming in from any country whatever under paragraph (d) had to pay a specific duty of 2\ cents for an eight ounce box or under. Now, what are the facts? When this protection was given the kippered herring industry a few years ago the Norwegians could not compete with our Canadian products unless they reduced the size of their container. I do not mean competing in the matter of duty, but in the matter of trade and commerce. They could not sell their goods in Canada in competition with our own kippered herrings on a four-ounce basis, because if they put up a four-ounce can they had to pay the specific duty on eight ounces, since the item covered containers of eight ounces or less.
When they saw that our product could be put in four or five ounce tins and sold at retail for five cents-the poor man's cheap food-the Norwegian government undertook to see if they could not have a change made. An appeal was made to the government under the favoured nation treaty, with the result that it was changed from a specific to an

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
ad valorem duty. It may be argued that the duty is higher on the ad valorem basis and that therefore the protection should be greater, but such is not the case. An ad valorem duty of 30 per cent on the goods heretofore imported into Canada from Norway would not be so great as the specific duty, having regard to the way the goods are put up. Therefore when it is put on an ad valorem basis on a four ounce can, you are lessening the protection to our own industry. On a can selling at 3i cents wholesale the protection on an ad valorem basis will be less than one cent, whereas under the specific duty, on the class of goods Norway is putting up to compete with our Canadian kippered herring, the duty is over two cents. Therefore we are lessening the protection afforded our own industry and opening the door to keen competition from a foreign country.
This is not carrying out the policy laid down by the present government. While I am not a believer in high protection, I am a believer in protection to a certain extent, and since the government has adopted the policy of protecting our own industries I am asking that they stand by that policy. Why should they so arrange the duty on kippered herring that it is the only kind of fish which does not bear a specific duty? Why should they place it on an ad valorem basis in order to permit Norway to compete with our own industry? When kippered herring was put on a specific basis some two or three years ago those interested in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick made very large expenditures in order to prepare themselves to compete in the world market. One firm alone spent over $60,000 for that purpose; they are putting up their kippered herring in an elongated can, for the right to use which they had to pay over $10,000 to an American concern. They have gone into this business in good faith, but this change to an ad valorem basis will permit the Norwegian product to come into keen competition with these firms in Canada and will place them in a position where they will not be able to carry on in the same way.
I have already placed this matter before the Prime Minister, though not in detail. He was kind enough to give me a few moments of his time; I knew he was a very busy man and we did not discuss the matter at any length. Now I would ask him, before finally passing that item, to go into it once more. He may reply that he has already gone into it, but he has not looked at it in the way I have presented it to-day. It may be said that these people are complaining before they are hurt, but let me say that we know our business as far as fish is concerned. In the
maritimes, and especially in New Brunswick, we take second place to no one in ascertaining how a duty of this kind will affect our business, and I am prepared to state that a thorough investigation into this question will prove my contention. I am quite ready to leave the investigation in the hands of officials of the Department of Fisheries instead of the Department of National Revenue; I am sure those officials will report that we are correct in the stand we are taking in this matter.
Let me go further; there should be no change in duty, under a protective policy, that will permit an outside nation to offer keener competition than has been the case in the past. If you are to give a fair show to our people, in competition with the other nations of the world, why should you allow an outside country to compete under a system which is adverse to those of our own people who produce similar goods. It is said that we have entered into world competition in connection with kippered herring, but it is not exactly world wide competition in the kippered herring branch of the fish industry. We have captured the principal markets of the world, as against Norway, in the sardine business; we have secured the entire Australian market, and we export sardines to some eighty-six other countries. Only within the last three years have we gone fully into the kippered herring business, and now the act of the government in changing the duty to an ad valorem basis will cripple that branch of the fishing industry in the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
knows that this matter was carefully considered by the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation. Much evidence was given before that board, the chief witness on behalf of the industry in question being Mr. McLean, who admitted that in some instances the protection was in excess of 100 per cent. Last year, as the hon. gentleman will remember, the rate was I7i per cent, 27i per cent and 30 per cent, but the department ruled that this class of sardines should come under item 120 and carry a specific duty, to which reference was made, and it carried the rate that was embodied in the tariff of last September.
When that rate was published the Norwegian consul general indicated that his country would appeal from that decision as to classification. Norway has a treaty with this country somewhat older than the country itself, I believe, and they enjoy favoured nation treatment. The matter proceeded, and I personally explained to him that in view of

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am referring to the
consul general for Norway, who protested against the ruling of the department. He came to Ottawa and presented his case again, and an investigation indicated that as the item now stands it carries a rate of approximately 90 per cent.
But it does not apply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It carries that rate-the
ad valorem rate which existed before September last, except by ruling of the department, in connection with the obtaining of which perhaps the hon. gentleman is fully informed The rate now is something over 90 per cent, in addition to which there is incidental protection in connection with the various matters that go into the production of the commodity in question. My memory is that Mr. McLean in giving his evidence before the tariff board-I speak subject to correction-stated that they carried on their export business in ninety countries in competition with this very product. Obviously we endeavoured to adjust this rate so as not to imperil the trade which by contract we had with Norway, while at the same time according a protection that amounts, as a matter of fact, to something over 90 per cent, which was the rate that existed before September last, until such time as the new ruling was made by the department, against which the Norwegian government protested and which we validated in order that no question of that kind might arise. We assured the government of Norway that we would consider the matter in the meantime, and as a result of that consideration it is felt that the original proposal, which carried a rate of over 90 per cent, is not unreasonable in view of the evidence given by Mr. McLean himself before the tariff board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is because they
are not sardines.

Ours are sardines. The
name sardine is derived from the fact that these smaller fish were caught near the island of Sardinia. That is how sardines got their name. But the question now being considered by experts is this: Is a sardine a herring or is a herring a sardine? That question has not yet been settled. The great bulk of the business we are doing throughout the world is being carried on under the name of sardine. The kippered herring is in a different class altogether from what are known as sardines. Kippered herrings are not known on the market as sardines; they are altogether different. What was commonly known as the smoked herring was a business largely carried on years ago in the maritime provinces, but owing to improved methods, specializing in the kippered herring, many Nova Scotian and New Brunswick producers went out of business. Under the new system, however, they are trying to come back into the business. They are adopting a new method of producing kippered herring, and it is an injustice to the business of New Brunswick that any change should be made so as to give an undue advantage to Norway in competition with our own people, notwithstanding the favoured nations treaty. England has never attempted to change that treaty between France and themselves to help us. Why should we change our system of protection to our own people in order to favour Norway, especially when there is nothing in the favoured nations clause that gives them the right to come here and appeal against our decision? They may protest; but where have they the right to appeal against a decision of that kind? They may enter a protest, have conversations and carry on negotiations with Canada in regard to the duty. But I insist that they have no right to enter an appeal. No country has the right to appeal against any decision of the House of Commons in regard to its tariff policy.

Ways and, Means-Cusloms Tariff
What should we look like if we went to the United States and appealed against any decision of theirs? To-day we have a favoured nation treaty with Norway. If they imposed certain high duties against us, could we go there and appeal? We might discuss the matter with them, but that is all we could do. If they can show us reasons why we should not follow a certain course in this matter, then we can consider their representations. But, I repeat, Norway has no right under the treaty to appeal from any decision we may make in regard to our tariff.
With regard to kippered herring in sealed containers, not touching the question of sardines, under what item does the minister expect this article to come after he has struck it out of 120?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It will come under 123.

That is what I was thinking. The hon. member for Gloucester suggested 121, but that is fish preserved in oik. I agree with the minister. With regard to the attitude of the Norwegian government, I understand that they protested under their treaty. Have they a treaty which gives them more favourable terms than the British preferential tariff? Even if they demanded the British preferential tariff they would still be subject to 120.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps I should amplify this matter. My hon. friend from Gloucester said, with perfect clearness, that it was contended that a kippered herring was not a sardine, nor was a sardine a kippered herring. That was exactly the attitude of the Norwegian government. Their contention was that a kippered herring could not carry the rate charged against sardines, in which class it was prior to September. That is the whole question, and the very argument which the hon. member for Gloucester has now made is the argument that was made by representatives of the Norwegian government-that you could not classify these two under the same general designation. The board of customs arrived at a conclusion. The rates theretofore were 17-J per cent, 27j per cent and 30 per cent; and the producers in this country having prosecuted their claim with vigour, the department accepted their view and put a specific duty on kippered herring, classified within the sardine category. Against that the government of Norway protested. As I have said, we validated it last fall for the sake of regularity of administration, assuring them at the time that they would have ample opportunity to discuss the matter at length, which they did. The representations which
my hon. friend has made to me personally have been made by the industry itself as well as in the evidence given before the tariff board, which I fancy has been read by most hon. gentlemen. Representations were also made by Scotch fishermen. As the matter stands, we believe this will afford reasonable protection to the industry in Canada. I need hardly assure the committee that I would be the last man in the world to do anything which would adversely affect an industry in Canada, much less one in New Brunswick. I would point out to my hon. friend that he is in error in assuming for a single moment that the government of Norway undertook to indicate to us that our parliament meant to do what it did last fall.
What about the basis of appeal?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Under the statute they had the right of appeal to the governor in council after the matter had been considered by the customs board. The hon. gentleman is thoroughly familiar with the circumstances and he must realize that it is in the interests of administration that it should not be arbitrarily declared that kippered herring comes within the sardine item. It could not be administered in that way without some statutory authority. When the statutory authority was granted it was indicated that the representations made would be studied. Evidence was given before the advisory board and as a result it is believed that ample security will be afforded to our own industry while at the same time there will be removed the grievances which the Norwegian government had presented both to our predecessors and to us, and which were threatening the friendly trade relations which existed between the two countries.
Why not put herring in the same class as kippered herring? A herring is not a sardine, so why leave it under the specific clause? Norway is not competing against us in the herring line.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend knows better than I that the general conclusions of one group of scientists is that all these fish should be classified as herring. He is quite right in saying that the classification of sardines is what caused the difficulty in the exporting of our herring into Great Britain. This difficulty became rather acute and if my memory serves me right, under the old Cobden commercial treaty-

That was in 1854.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. Under that treaty they were given admission into Great Britain as sardines. It was agreed that practically a monopoly existed with respect to French sardines, and the contention now made is that from a technical standpoint these are not sardines at all, they are only herring. It is needless to say that they sell much more readily by being designated as sardines. The question of kippered herring and sardines became rather acute at one time, and we believe that this classification will indicate quite clearly that 'like competition shall be met with like rates, that herring shall compete with herring, sardines with sardines and kippered herring with kippered herring. When I was a boy they were called Digby chicken; they were small smoked herring put up in wooden boxes. Then the herring was put up in oil after being smoked, and was called snacks or kippered herring. Only a few days ago I had an opportunity of seeing samples of the Norwegian and Canadian packages. The one is an elongated package, while the other is more rectangular. I cannot help but think that our domestic producers are more worried than the circumstances would warrant. The cost laid down of the Norwegian product is not less than 3i cents, and I think it sells at five cents, so that there is a reasonable measure of protection.
I do not wish to delay the committee nor do I want to attempt to draw a herring across the trail.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: A kippered herring.

From the experience which I have gained in the administration of the customs, in connection with the fisheries of my own province, and my knowledge of the method of doing this work, I am convinced that I am right. I am going to leave it at that because by the next session of this house we will have an opportunity of seeing just what takes place. If I am right I hope that the department will change its attitude.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I hasten to assure the
hon. gentleman that if there is an increase in price, there will at once be a reduction in duty. There is an absolute guarantee against an increase in price.

Why is such a terrific increase in duty imposed if it is intended to remove it if the slightest advantage is taken of it? One cannot disabuse one's mind of the idea that there must be some reason for such a heavy increase. Yet we are told in the next breath that if there is any increase over present-day prices the whole increase in duty will be wiped off. If there were an increase of 20 or 25 per cent, one could understand the matter, but when an increase of this character is imposed one cannot but be forced to the conclusion that some advantage will be taken of it or there would be no necessity for it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I tried to tell the committee the other day, and I shall continue to state as we proceed with respect to a very large number of items:	The increase is subject to the criticism which the hon. gentleman has suggested, namely, that it is a very large increase, but it arises on account of the emergent conditions under which the industry is now functioning. The slaughter of our market to-day, three months, four months from now, has the effect of discouraging business in the future and, in the end, the utter destruction of business. The government has intimated that if this structure of ours that I and others found here is to be maintained, there must be no increase to the consumer
of the price that is charged, but we are perfectly willing, as I tried to make clear to the committee the other day, and, more than that, anxious to ensure that Canadians should have this market. This is an endeavour to meet the situation. I might say that the manufacturers asked for a much larger increase than that in view of their own experience of which they gave us a record, namely, the slaughtering in this market at given moments, not frequent, but just sufficiently often to imperil the stability of the market and the maintenance of Canadian industry. That is the reason for the action taken. I have met the situation frankly, and I tell my hon. friend what has been done has been done not by accident, but with deliberation and for a purpose which is quite clear and which I have no hesitancy in expressing.

I think my hon. friend is somewhat safe in making the prediction, although one cannot tell what the fluctuations in price will be, that prices on secondary products will not increase, at least in the immediate future. Rather, indeed, they should go down, following the trend of the primary products. The spread is too great. Why in the world, in the face of a situation such as that, we need such excessive rates of duty, I confess I cannot understand, particularly as the government have very drastic authority to prevent dumping. The fixation of price is a weapon which they can use any day. While manufacturers can get behind duties such as my right hon. friend is imposing, there is bound to be a tendency to take advantage of them. I venture the assertion now without much fear of contradiction, that had it not been for the increases in duty last September in connection with textiles and other products, prices would have been lower in Canada to-day. The manufacturers have promised not to increase the price, but the protection which they enjoy by excessive rates of duty gives them the advantage of maintaining their products at a price level not warranted by the trend of events so far as manufacturing production is concerned. That is my complaint against these excessive rates of duty. This is a food product that everybody, particularly in western Canada and I presume in other parts of the country as well, must use. Why there is a necessity for such an excessive rate of duty as this I cannot understand.

As the minister well

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for Medicine Hat has referred to a matter that required no argument on his part to convince me of the importance that should attach to it. I was privileged many years ago to do something towards establishing a beet sugar industry in the irrigation belt near Calgary. There is now at Raymond an industry which has flourished, but which has recently been acquired by the eane sugar interests. There was a beet sugar industry in eastern Canada; I think there were two in the county of Kent, and they have been acquired by cane sugar companies. The question as to just what assistance can be given and how it can be given to the beet sugar industry is one that is not as easy of solution as it appears. If it were, I am satisfied that my hon. friends opposite would have solved it years ago. It has been complicated in recent years by reason of the West Indian treaty. We have endeavoured by that treaty to ensure the purchase of our sugar requirements in the raw state from British possessions. A part of that sugar will undoubtedly come from Australia; a part has come from the Fiji islands; another portion of it has come from another part of the world in the Far East, and a large portion has recently come from the West Indies. The hon. gentleman is quite right in what he says with respect to Cuban sugar. The real truth is that Cuban importations have had the effect of Very seriously injuring the sugar refining business in Canada. I suppose the hon. gentleman saw in the newspapers a few days ago a case in point. The truth is that sugar from Cuba has been dumped on our market at a tremendously low price, so low that our beet sugar people could not meet it at all. I had very definitely concluded that a bonus should be given to the beet sugar industry. I was

satisfied from representations made that that was the only method by which we could ensure the development of the irrigation areas south o,f Medicine Hat and east of Calgary, a great district which has been settled in a small way but which might easily be settled in a much larger way. To my regret I found that it was not possible to carry into effect the idea I had in my mind, and having regard to our treaty obligations and other matters to which I have referred I need hardly tell the committee that what I would have been doing, had the original thought in my mind been given effect to, would be to bonus the cane sugar refineries.
Beet sugar?

It seems to me that it may be almost impossible for them to do so unless very considerable assistance is afforded by the government. I can only say to the hon. gentleman that I have not abandoned hope that some satisfactory solution may be found, but in all frankness, having regard to our treaty obligations with respect to the West Indies and to the ownership by the same interests of both the refineries and the factories in the centre west, we are faced with a matter of extreme difficulty. speechtext:
Certainly not. The hon. member knows, perhaps as well as any member of this committee, that the economic stress has greatly decreased manufacturing production, and he doubtless knows that the unpaid liabilities for implements, due not only to Canadian producers but to producers outside Canada who have maintained branches in this country, amount to millions of dollars, and that at the moment there have been practically no purchases at all of agricultural implements in western Canada. It is obvious that a reduction in price can come about only if there is a demand for the article produced, for the cost of production will not decrease materially until increased requirements lower the unit cost of production. It is one of those matters which I am sure the hon. member thoroughly understands and which works in a complete circle. On the one hand you desire to obtain a reduction in the

cost of production, and on the other hand it is not possible unless there is an increased demand for the manufactured article; and until there is such an increased demand as will enable the factories to operate at a lower cost per unit how are you going to get a decrease in price? In the meantime while raw materials may decrease in value, that decrease is more than offset by the increase on the unit cost of production, brought about by a curtailment of production due to the economic depression through which we are passing.

In other words, it means that the only man who will be able to go through this economic depression will be the man who can hide behind the tariff. It cannot mean anything else. If the lack of business has increased the cost of production of the manufacturing industry to the extent the Prime Minister has intimated, and the manufacturer is going to make up that increased cost of production by putting the tariff on the price of his commodities, then we are back to the statement that has been made in this, house time and again since I have been a member-that the agricultural industry and other consumers will absorb the whole depression. I do not see how it can be otherwise, if the Prime Minister's argument is sound, that through the depression having resulted in a lower volume of business the cost of production in our factories has increased, and consequently the prices of manufactured commodities will not go down materially. I think I understand the Prime Minister's argument rightly; if not, I am ready to be corrected before I proceed further. If I am not corrected, then my interpretation of the Prime Minister's remarks must be all right. If the cost of production due to the depression which exists to-day has placed the manufacturer in that position; if that be true, as the Prime Minister has said, then the people who buy those manufactured commodities, the agriculturists and consumers generally, are paying for the whole depression which the manufacturing industry is suffering from to-day. I have made this statement before, and I repeat it. The Prime Minister knows it to be true probably better than anybody else, because having lived in the west he knows that the wheat grower, the butter producer and the stock man are not going to be able to continue to produce unless they are able to buy what they require at prices comparable with the prices they receive for their own products. I think it is just as well that the argument of the Prime Minister should go out to the country so the people 22110-235
may know that the farmers and the consumers generally are shouldering the burden of the manufacturers who are able to get behind the tariff.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If that is not bearing the burden I do not know What is. And this effort on their part to bear their share of the economic depression is met by statements such as that to which we have just listened 1 That is one of the difficulties in this country-an endeavour to arouse one section of the country against another-

I resent that statement.
Mr. BENNETT-an endeavour to make it appear that the agriculturist is suffering and someone else is getting the entire benefit. In my judgment that is not rendering any service to the country. In this period of distress it is quite obvious that the over-production of cereals was reflected in the tremendous reduction in prices, because last December there was sufficient wheat in the world to meet the requirements of the entire consuming population for twenty months, with no further production. That was the statistical evidence. The reduction in the price of wheat as a commodity is well known to every member of the committee, and that diminution in the selling price is reflected at once, of course, in the -diminution in purchasing power on the part of those among whom the money circulates. If the producer of primary products is not able to purchase his implements, of course it follows that the manufacturer has his interest charges running against his inventory, which he cannot reduce. There is no doubt about that, and in turn he must absorb that loss; we have

say is that it is impossible with respect to people who for three successive seasons have had no crops; of course nothing could be as bad as that except the destruction of an industry by fire, without insurance. I resent any lecture from the Prime Minister accusing anyone on this side of the house, myself in particular, of trying to hurt any industry. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) realizes the great difficulty there would be in bonusing an industry in a particular locality, or in limiting the operation of such legislation. It is that difficulty which has stood in the way of something being done at the present session. Bonuses and bounties which heretofore have been limited to apply to particular industries, such as the lead bounties and copper bounties, would in this case operate over a very wide area, namely the provinces of Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario. I should be very glad to listen to any suggestion the hon. member may have to make by which we could work out a scheme to accomplish the end he has in view.
