speechtext: It depends on the value of the importation and the weight. I should like to say very frankly to the committee that this item represents a deliberate effort to maintain the silk industry. There are several small silk plants in Canada. They are manufacturing, I think, as economically and efficiently as any industries in this country. They have a substantial capital investment and in the very nature of things give employment to a large number of people as compared with the entire value of the product. I have reason to believe that the interests largely concerned in the success of similar enterprises in the United States have substantial stock holdings in these enterprises. I am further advised, and I am certain from my investigations, that under existing conditions they could put their product into this country and stop the activities of our mills. I have on my desk samples of the products of both the mills south of us and in Canada and of those in other countries. The mill at Louiseville, Quebec, is one of the industries to which I refer; that is not wholly, but in part, common ownership. There are others similarly situated, and after hearing what had to be said and investigating the matter as fully as possible, having regard to the apparent effort on the part of those who had substantial inventories in other countries to find here, if possible, a market, we concluded that it was desirable to maintain this industry, for reasons that I think are fairly apparent. The action indicated by the item in the tariff is the action which we believe will serve that purpose.
What were the importations last year and from what countries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The importations were 8,240,000 yards, valued at $4,366,000, of which $1,731,000 worth came from the United States and nearly $1,500,000 from Japan.

If I understood the Prime Minister aright he has revealed a most amazing situation. We have been told that it is desirable so to adjust our tariff that American manufacturers will establish branch factories in this country. Now we are told that certain American manufacturers who have established branch factories in Canada for the manufacture of silk will close them unless we raise our tariff still higher and allow them to make a still greater profit from their Canadian factories, out of the pockets of the Canadian people, to be taken to the United States. That is an amazing situation. I do not think we should tolerate it for one moment- to induce factories to come here by a high tariff, and then have them tell us that unless we give them a higher tariff they will close down and throw their workmen out of employment I should like to ask the Prime Minister how many people are employed in the factories; what is the total wage bill; what percentage of the product represents wage costs; what is the duty he expects to lose by shutting out these products, and any other information which will give us a clear understanding of what this will cost us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Might I ask the hon. gentleman to be good enough to read from his book the answer to the questions he has asked?
Mr. Y'OUNG: I only have some notes here which I jotted down while my right hon. friend was talking.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has the information.
Mr. Y'OUNG: Where?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Right beside him, as I understand it.
No, I have not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I thought my hon. friend told me he had it. I have not the information that has been requested; I did not undertake to prepare it with respect to all the industries in Canada. But my hon. friend did not quite follow me. I did not say they controlled the industry, but that they had an interest in it, and that they also had an industry in the United States. There are

IFfij/s and Means-Customs Tariff
several thousand people employed in the industry in Canada, scattered over the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I have not before me at the moment the exact number, nor have I brought other information with me, because we are dealing with only one phase of the industry, not the whole of it. If it is desired, the item could stand until the information is forthcoming.
I think it would be. well if we had that information, because to my mind this is one of the very extravagant increases in this schedule, amounting to almost 100 per cent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Depending on the value.

In the
cheaper lines of silk it runs to approximately 100 per cent. There are mills already established under the existing protection, and I fail to understand the necessity for this very drastic increase in tariff. I should like to know how many people are employed in this industry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I shall be quite content to have the item stand. Perhaps my hon. friend has that information before him, in his brief.
No, I have not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I can get it for the industry as a whole. I am sure the hon. gentleman understands that it cannot be segregated.
We are asking for the information having to do with that part of the silk industry covered by this drastic increase.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot give the information in respect to the portion of the industry covered by this item, but with respect to the silk industry as a whole, last year the silk production in this country was valued at in the vicinity of $12,000,000, speaking from memory. This is an exceptional condition now prevailing; it is really an emergency. I quite agree with what the hon. gentleman has said; the rate is very high as compared with the present rate, but I may tell my hon. friend what one of the gentlemen who came to us said to me about it. He said, "I am in this business in the United States in a very large way. My people have a small interest in Canada, only in one place. In the United States we have taken steps to prevent the importation of these goods by rates of 55, 60 and 65 per cent, and unless some action is taken, with our surplus inventories in the United States your mere dumping duty will

not be sufficient to shut out these goeds." Of course there are very large importations from countries other than the United States. After the matter was very carefully gone into it was realized that a specific duty was necessary in addition to an ad valorem duty, unless we imposed an ad valorem duty that seemed out of all proportion to what such a duty should be. Those are the facts of the matter, as it stands.

So you are
putting on'a specific duty in order to deceive the people and not let them know the cost?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, to give them knowledge.
Did I understand my right hon. friend to say that this was an American who came with this information?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, he said he came
from New York.
And he asked that the Canadian duty be raised?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, he presented the
situation as it wras. He did not ask for an increase in the duty; he put it in this way, that he had confidence in the intelligence of the Canadian people who desired to protect this industry from destruction, and I am inclined to think he was right.
This American is very much interested in Canadian industry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, he said quite frankly what I afterwards found to be true. I might correct my hon. friend's statement in regard to the money being made, because this industry has not yet made money. This gentleman fold me he would make much more money if he were able to supply Canadian requirements from his mills in the United States, and it did not require very much arithmetic to see why fhat should be so. But, having made an investment here, not in his own company but in a stock investment which is rather widely held, he and his associates believed that the Canadian people would be interested in knowing what was the situation; from other sources I took the trouble to verify his statements, and this is the result. I hardly expected that it would commend itself to my hon. friend, but I still believe that in this time of stress we cannot afford to let that industry, employing several thousand people, suffer. One of the people who came to me represented a plant in the Welland district near St. Catharines, I believe, and he made the position perfectly clear. The other application, as I say, was from this gentleman from New York. He did not come with any group of people; he simply

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
came up on the train and said, "Here is the position as to costs, and here is our position as to sales. We would be better off financially if we could supply the Canadian market from our American plants." I saw at once the force of that argument, because they could keep their large plants going to capacity, and would be much better off in that way. We chose this course.

My right hon. friend says
this gentleman told him that he would make more money by supplying the Canadian market from his American factories, but he knew perfectly well that if the tariff were lowered so that the American product could enter, the products of factories in France, Germany and other countries could enter also. He wanted high protection so his Canadian branch factory could enjoy a monopoly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He has not a monopoly,
and I am sure my hon. friend knows that. There is no relation between the Welland plant and the other plant mentioned; they are competitors. One of the real objections urged against this tariff was what I daresay my hon. friend saw in the newspapers, that we had too many silk factories in Canada, that competition had grown too keen, and that they could not expect to make much money because ten million people could not absorb the products of the number of mills there are in this country. That was the position taken by some people. I put to my hon. friend the converse of the position which he took.

Let us accept that statement; let us say there are too many factories in Canada to have all their products absorbed by the Canadian people. What is the remedy? There is only one; that is to reduce production costs to the point where these products can be exported in order to capture some of the world market.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Our best hope of capturing some of the world' market is to have a market at home. We shall capture some of the world market, as we have done in a small way, but we cannot hope to do so extensively unless we can produce something at unit rates of cost comparable with those of competing countries. As matters now stand, I think my hon. friend will agree that unless some such action as this is taken we shall certainly not have a silk industry in Canada.
If with the duty at present in force we cannot have a silk industry in Canada, then it seems to me it is a pretty expensive luxury.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Under present economic conditions, with distress sales all over the country, I Should like the Committee to understand my view of the situation. Every business man opposite me, if he will take the trouble to investigate, will arrive at exactly the conclusion I have reached. This is an age, not of competition in production but of competition in reducing inventories; and in the effort to reduce inventories prices have been disregarded and commodities offered on a basis not heretofore thought possible. Now we have to conclude what action we shall take, not starting at the very threshold of these undertakings, but facing the fact that the undertakings are with us. For instance, the silk industry was not established last fall, nor the fall before that. It has existed in Canada for many years, having been slowly developed. Whether hon. gentlemen opposite or we ourselves, facing the issue to-day, would decide upon developing a silk industry in Canada, I cannot answer. I am sure some hon. gentlemen opposite would say it was not desirable; I am sure some of us on this side would say the same. But the fact is that the industry is here; the investment has been made.
We have the raw product for rayon silk.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is a separate thing. In this industry we had last year a production amounting to S12,000,000, and under the tariff of 1928, 810.000,000. I put to the committee the question I had to ask myself, and the only answer I could give was that I was not prepared to see the industry destroyed. I ask one question further: What- action may I take in this emergent condition as will ensure the maintenance of the industry without permitting exploitation? What the committee sees before it is about as reasonable as we can do under the circumstances, high though it looks. I actually had in my desk- I should not care to say where they came from-samples from various countries, and the fact is that the price at which one of these articles, similar to one produced in this country, can be produced abroad represents just 50 per cent of what it costs to produce here.
Does not the dumping clause take care of that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. I asked myself that very question. The hon. gentleman is a man of business, and I could point out to him many cases in which the dumping clause will not effect the purpose we have in mind. That is why we put in force the section to which

I)T ayn and Means-Customs Tariff
I referred the other day. I know of no other way to save the situation in the present emergency. This is not being done for the sake of doing it. If I thought there was any other method by which it could be done, my colleagues and I would not take this course. But because we can see no other way we are bound to proceed as we are doing. Not that we might choose to create this industry if we had the power to determine that. But the industry is here and I am not prepared to take the responsibility of seeing it destroyed.
Perhaps I may tell the Prime Minister what information we should like to have. We want to have the total investment in Canada,-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That might be difficult
to get.

-the number of employees, the salaries and wages paid, the cost of raw material, the percentage of the total product paid in wages, total production, total imports, duty collected, and the number of factories which are under American control.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With respect to the last question, I am afraid I cannot satisfy the hon. gentleman's laudable curiosity. I observe that the questions he has put are in the sequence in which they appear in the last year book. I shall therefore endeavour to transfer to a sheet of paper the information contained in -the year book and read it to the committee.

Does this discussion relate
to the silk industry as a whole?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Gloucester will perhaps have heard the observation of the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) that the rayon industry is entirely different; and the celanese industry depends on the chemical action of certain acids on cotton and wood. The experiments now being carried on at Drummondville and in the United States seem to indicate the possibility at an early date of treating wood in such a way that it may take the place of cotton. I believe the experiments have been reasonably successful and that we may soon expect wood properly treated chemically to be the raw material of both rayon and celanese. This item refers to what might be called the silk industry as distinguished from the artificial silk industry. My remarks had reference to an industry the raw material for which is imported.

There appeared in La Presse of Saturday, May 2, an interview with Mr. 
Brupbaeher, manager of the Brupbacher Silk Mills, Limited, Valleyfield. Mr. Brupbacher said :
A just protection established on a basis of equity cannot but help all industries of all countries. Canada will lose nothing by continuing this principle.
He goes on to give data with regard to this industry in Canada:
The rapid expansion of the silk industry in Canada during the last eight years constitutes one of the major points of the economic development of our country. In 1922 Canada had seven factories. In 1928 this number reached twenty-two. The capital invested increased from $4,618,448 to $28,278,656. Our factory is the youngest in Canada.
This is one of the factories for the establishment of which credit was given to the new tariff. As a matter of fact, its construction began in May 1930, at the time the Dunning budget was introduced. According to this authority on silk manufacture in Canada, under a moderate tariff the silk industry has succeeded. In seven years it has increased its invested capital from nearly $5,000,000 to a little over $28,000,000. This gentleman, who is one of the founders of the silk industry-in Canada, is certainly not asking for greater protection. It might be well to consider that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Nothing could more
clearly demonstrate the difficulty of the situation than the item which the hon. member has just read, a copy of which is on the files in the department. I said to the committee, what any hon. member can abundantly satisfy himself upon, that there was no break in domestic prices, with respect to many of the inventories of goods such as this, until as a matter of fact very recently. This is what happens in every crisis.
This was in May, 1931.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The crisis has occurred
in Europe and there comes a time when the peak is reached and there is either a breaking up or an improvement. The position I desire to make clear to this committee is one I would like hon. members opposite, especially the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Young) to look into between now and to-morrow in order to satisfy themselves of what I have said. The inventories held by the silk and allied concerns were very considerable. Most of these companies did not believe that the economic crisis through which the world was passing would reach anything like the acute stage it has reached at the present time. They held on hoping against hope that they would not be compelled to sacrifice the price of their domestic production, but alas there

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
came a time when other countries would not absorb their surplus production at any price, and the price of inventories dropped As a matter of fact the situation in May was not anything like it is in July, and in July it is worse than it was last month. The resolutions of which I will give notice tonight contain specific modifications; I only wish I did not have to take this action, but I am convinced as to the necessity.

The right hon. member
states that this extremely high duty is being placed upon this commodity in order to meet an emergency which has arisen since May. How does he expect to meet the situation if the emergency disappears during the next four or five months?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Under the general statute we have the right to reduce duties.
I know that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And that action has been taken before. If it were not that I and my colleagues were convinced of the necessity, the time of the committee would not be taken up in this regard. I do not blame any party for the condition which exists, but I believe the duty is cast upon the government to see that this industry is not destroyed. The provisions of the law are such that we cannot increase a duty by order in council, but reduction can be made. I commend this to the committee.
There is no other method of meeting this emergency?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Prices for duty could be fixed. That would be exercising the third power I mentioned a few days ago, which was vested in the executive by the legislation of last fall. Hon. members opposite have, not unfairly, criticized that form of action-
It is the law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is a form of the law
which we will use as little as possible.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I say that to my hon.
friend. If it were not for my firm belief as to the necessity, it would not be there, but being there we will use it as little as possible. Land my colleagues felt that the proper place to deal with this matter was in this committee. We felt that the committee should be told the exact position and be asked for its judgment.
The budget was submitted on June 1, and these various items were part of the budget. The emergency referred to by the right hon. gentleman did not exist on June 1.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes, it did.

There may have been some threat of it, but there certainly was no such emergency on June 1 when the budget was submitted. There was no such emergency existing at the time the interview to which I referred took place, and no change occurred between that time and the introduction of the budget on June 1. I am not convinced that the right hon. gentleman is correct when he says that this high tariff has been put into effect in order to meet an emergency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In any event the item is
to stand.

The right hon. gentleman ha3 stated that our silk manufacturers, thinking the depression had reached the bottom and that prices would not go down any lower, held their goods off the market in the hope of being able to realize higher prices.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say the manufacturers in Canada; I said out of Canada.
Not in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I tried to make it clear that the manufacturers in other countries had enormous inventories which they are now attempting to push into this country or any other country in which it would be possible to gain entry for their goods. I ask my hon. friend to interview any merchant who has to do with these matters and find out what his experience has been during the last six weeks. My hon. friend's information is my information.
Would my right hon. friend tell the committee whether the Canadian manufacturers had large inventories?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have asked that the item should stand in consequence of what the hon. member said.
Could the minister give the committee an idea of the range of prices of fabrics included in this item?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My recollection is that it runs from 40 cents per yard, or perhaps a little less, up to something like $5 per yard.

It strikes me that a duty of 10 cents per lineal yard on a silk selling for 40 cents per yard is altogether out of pro-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
portion to the same duty on silk selling at $5 per yard. There is a 25 per cent duty plus a 45 per cent duty, a total of 70 per cent which the poor person has to pay when buying a fabric costing 40 cents per yard as against the same duty per yard which is paid by the fortunate person able to pay $5 per yard for the fabric he purchases. It seems to me unfair that in one case the duty should be ten times as much as in the other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this committee is fertile in resource and I would ask it what suggestion it has to make in order to deal with the facts which I have outlined and which the committee can verify for itself, member for member. What suggestion has any hon. member to make with respect to a specific duty in addition to the ad valorem duty? The first suggestion was to apply the duty by weight; it was found that that would not work out. The next suggestion wa3 to apply it according to the fineness of the texture of the fabric, as is the case with some of the woollen items; that was rejected. The next suggestion was to take length as the standard or yardstick; that one has been adopted. If the committee can suggest a better one, I hasten to assure it that I shall endeavour in anyway in my power to see that it is adopted.
Is there any necessity for adopting a specific duty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Aes; in view of the circumstances to which I have alluded, I see no other way of dealing with the matter.

Before the textile items are all put through, I should like to place before, the committee the condition of another branch of the textile industry, namely, the knitted goods industry. When the duty was raised last fall on different classes of textiles, there is no doubt this was a great benefit to various branches of the industry. As an example I may say that my Liberal opponent in the last campaign is engaged in the. textile industry and at the time of the election that industry was working four days a week and short hours. The last I have heard about it is that since the duty was raised last fall, it is working twenty-four hours a day and six days in the week. That, however, is not the case with the knitted goods industry. When the duty was raised on other branches of the industry last fall, owing to the provisions of the French treaty it was impossible to accord the same 
treatment to the. knitted goods industry. Schedule D of the French treaty sets the duty on knitted goods at 25 per cent and because of that it prevents any increase in the British preferential rate, as the rate on British goods cannot, of course, be any higher than that on similar foreign goods. In addition to that it prevents any increase in the tariff on this class of goods from some twenty-one other countries which enjoy the privileges of the French treaty. These countries include Japan and Czechoslovakia. The last available figures which I have for imports of this class of goods are as follow's, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1930:
Country	Amounts
United Kingdom	 $1,815,000
All countries	 2,916,000
France	 110,000
As the amount imported from France is only $110,000, the provision of the French treaty setting the duty at 25 per cent is of no immediate advantage to France, because only a very limited amount comes from that country, but at the same time is a very great disadvantage to the Canadian industry and to Canadian workers.
The artificial silk knitted industry is in the same situation as that of other knitted goods. Artificial silk yarns are coming into Canada to-day at a higher rate of duty than artificial silk knitted goods. For that reason it is increasingly difficult for the knitted goods industry to operate and carry on. I think in justice to the knitted goods industry some change should be made that would make it possible for the present administration to accord the same treatment to that portion of the textile industry as is being accorded to every other part of it.
Item stands.
Customs tariff-569c. Hat braids, of a class or kind not made in Canada, whether woven, knitted or plaited, not exceeding four inches in w'idth, imported for use exclusively in the manufacture of hat bodies or shapes, but not for use in the ornamentation or trimming of such bodies or shapes, under regulations prescribed by the minister: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tari, free.

speechtext: Purely as an administrative matter, and to remove any possible doubt, I wish to add to this item the words "from wood."

Customs tariff-597. Pianofortes and organs: British preferential tariff, 20 per cent; intermediate tariff, 27J per cent; general tariff, 30 per cent.
Provided, that when imported under the intermediate or general tariff the duty shall be not less than, each: British preferential tariff, ... .; intermediate tariff, $75; general tariff, $75.

I notice there is a duty of 30 per cent under the general tariff, with a minimum of S75. That is to say, if a piano valued at $200 enters Canada, the duty would be $60, but there is a special provision which says that it must be not less than $75. That is another way of saying that the cheaper piano shall carry a higher rate of duty than the more expensive one. In that there is a discrimination against the poorer people who cannot buy expensive instruments. In view of what the Prime Minister told us the other day regarding the situation in the piano industry, could he not do something for that industry by making pianos cheaper and thus bringing more buyers into the market?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: To make pianos cheaper would mean that they would come from some other country than Canada. The hon. gentleman can satisfy himself, by going to the factories in Montreal or cities in Ontario, that the actual cost of the materials that enter into the production of a piano of the cheaper kind represents more money than the price at which, for the reasons I indicated a few minutes ago, they are now being offered for importation into Canada. I wonder if the hon. gentleman realizes that pianos are not dearer in Canada; they have become very much cheaper in the last few years. Of course there is a class of piano, the concert grand, that is highly expensive, costing thousands of dollars. We imported some of them last year from Germany. We have imported them from the United States. One of them made in Philadelphia has had a reputation for almost a century now. There is one of the same type made in New York state. What one might call a piano of general use is one that is being sold at a reasonable price in this country.
A cottage piano.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but recently they have been dumped into this country at a price which we cannot possibly meet. The piano people waited upon the government; they produced evidence of the cost in their own factories, and I have no hesitation in saying to hon. gentlemen that they will be glad to show them their methods of production. These factories are not nearly as active as they were before the radio came into general use.
Is that not the cause of a large part of their difficulty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As I said to my hon. friend the other day, I do not desire to minimize that. After all, however, $75, is as the committee will realize, 30 per cent on $250, and on the basis of reasonable value for the commodity offered, I think the committee will say that a reasonable price for the production of pianos would not be less than $250.
In Canada a fairly good piano would cost from $500 to $700.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Less than that.

My right hon. friend could not get a piano he would be any more than proud of for $700. A fairly good radio costs about $200. If a $200 radio is displacing a $600 or S700 piano the only possible way for the piano to gain ground is to find some means of reducing the price. Every measure taken to raise the prices of the piano places it under a still greater handicap as compared with the radio.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In connection with this item the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) will move an amendment to clarify a difficulty concerning colour, which was raised by some hon. members opposite. The amendment will read as follows:
605. Leather produced from East India tanned kip, uneoloured, or coloured other than black, when imported for use exclusively in lining boots and shoes; genuine reptile leathers: British preferential tariff, 124 per cent; intermediate tariff, 15 per cent; general tariff, 15 per cent.
Having had occasion to buy leather boots undoubtedly hon. members will know what kip is. Some difficulty arose with respect to the classification of this commodity, to overcome which the amendment adds the words "other than black." There is a special item with respect to the exception. The rates are not changed in the present amendment.
How is sole leather affected by these changes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Sole leather is dealt with by item 604, which has just passed. However if the hon. member desires information I shall be pleased to give it.

In view of the fact that the exports of sole leather are enormously larger than the imports, an increase of that kind would seem to be altogether unnecessary. The imports are trifling as compared with the exports.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I suppose the hon. member knows, as I should have stated with respect to another item this afternoon, that the action of our friends to the south has shut us out of that market entirely, with the result that we have to look to other markets.
We are not entirely shut out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not entirely, but largely, since last year.
What is the necessity for the change in the definition of the item?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The amendment adds the words "other than black," owing to the fact that the black leather is used for another purpose. There is no restriction of the use to which it might be put, because it is of a different quality and may be used for the

manufacture of the boots and shoes themselves as distinguished from the coloured kip which is used only for linings. The change may appear to be very slight, but it is one of importance.
The black leather carries a higher duty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
The hon. member has
been following the items, I am sure, with great care, and he will observe that the classifications have been rather narrow due to the fact that leather is a commodity of so many grades and qualities that necessarily attention must be paid not only to qualities but also to colours, as we noticed with respect to kip. Mr. YrOUNG: What is the object in charging 10 per cent under the general rate until a factory is established in Canada, at which time the rate jumps to 20 per cent, while there is no change in the British preferential or intermediate tariffs?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Because the competition will come from countries other than those covered by the British preferential and the intermediate tariff. In addition to that, the hon. gentleman will remember that we have endeavoured in this tariff revision not to make any changes in the British preference rates, and I think there are only one or two changes in the whole list. The reason was obvious. I think if my hon. friend will take a little trouble to look at the exporting countries, he will have no difficulty in seeing that this increase will become essential to maintain our industry if we develop it to the extent indicated by the proviso.
Will this change make any difference in the raw material of these glove makers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think I can satisfy my hon. friend from West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart). In reality it is a reduction. This is the first time the item has appeared in the tariff. In administration it was found that the leather garment lined with cotton paid

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
a duty on that basis, lined with wool it paid a duty on that basis, and lined with silk it paid duty on that basis; in other words, the linings determined the rates of duty. The rates now proposed are really a reduction. What is pointed out by my hon. friend is for the purpose of assisting the industry with respect to the importation of the raw material.

I can never understand why the consumer when he gets the raw material for his own use has to pay a higher duty than the manufacturer, particularly when I find the finished product carries an excessive rate of duty. Presumably there will not be any importation of the finished article because the high duty is imposed to prevent that, and the whole difference goes into the pockets of the manufacturer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The argument which the hon. gentleman has now made is one with which I am not unfamiliar, and members of the committee who read the reports of the tariff advisory board will find that argument frequently presented on behalf of the consumers league. It is an argument that should be directed to all countries which impose tariffs to develop their manufacturing industries. My hon. friend will find that from the very inception of tariffs in this country that general principle has been observed. I take it the desire was to stimulate industrial 'development, it not being thought likely that consumers would purchase in such quantities as to make them factors in such a market. I suppose other reasons might be given; for instance, drawbacks and rebates have been granted because export trade is conducted on a free trade basis. Great Britain has always allowed rebates or drawbacks, the United States has done so, and so have we.

I can well
understand the use of drawbacks because the manufacture of the goods exported gives employment to our own people, and consequently the country is benefited. But where the discrimination is against our own people, as it must be in cases of this kind, I have never been able to see the virtue of such treatment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is universal in its
application.

There is a point in connection with tariffs that applies very clearly to this particular item. I wonder whether it would be possible without destroying the tariff structure itself, to establish a graduated duty on such articles as leather

garments, and so forth, in order to induce the manufacturer to use Canadian raw material- hides, wool and other things. In that way it would pass on in some degree to the producer of raw material the benefit derived by the manufacturer from these tariffs. I think that might be a matter worthy of some consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has referred to something which, frankly, I should like to see applied, and I think he will find that one item in this tariff is a frank effort to apply it. In connection with automobiles my hon. friend will see, as we proceed to the end, an effort to apply that principle. It is a sound principle; there should be some incentive given to increase the use of our Canadian-produced materials, and I agree that it would be desirable to increase the use of the raw materials of this country in connection with the granting of tariff protection with respect to articles produced partly from domestic and partly from imported materials. As we deal with the item having to do with automobiles, not this evening but to-morrow, I would ask the hon. gentleman to remind me of this point, because I think he will find there an application in a small but effective way of the principle to which he refers.

I am glad to hear what the right hon. gentleman has said; I have often thought of that, particularly in connection with wool and leather goods, where a certain percentage of our own raw hides and wool could be used. For years our raw hides have been simply a drug on the market, thrown into a fence corner and allowed to rot. Certainly I would like to see that principle carried further and applied to some of the raw materials produced by our farmers, in order to give them a little taste of tariff advantage in that way.

I should be very sorry to see the suggestion of my hon. friend from Red Deer carried into effect. If we try to compel our Canadian manufacturers of leather goods to use Canadian leather, whether or not it suits their purposes, the people who buy those leather goods will suffer for it. In Canada we raise certain animals; their hides are useful for certain purposes, but not for other purposes. My hon. friend is a farmer. I wonder how he would like to buy a set of harness made from the side of a steer which grows heavy, thick hair, as compared to a set of harness made from the hide of a Texas steer which does not grow much hair at all.

Ways and, Means-CusLoms Tariff
He would find that it made a big difference in the quality of the harness.
In re^rd to the question of the exMinister of the Interior as to why there should be a higher rate on the finished article than on the half-finished article, I have just one observation to make. In the manufacturing process only about 50 per cent or less of the cost represents raw material, and when a manufacturer pays 20 per cent duty on his raw material he is paying that 20 per cent duty on half his production cost. But in selling his goods, if he gets only 20 per cent it is on the whole of his production cost. He has an advtange there, and when you give him a higher rate, say a rate of 35 per cent which you give here as against 20 per cent, you are giving him a double advantage which I think is quite unnecessary.

I might say that the remarks of my hon. friend from Weyburn are perfectly correct, but those facts were so obvious that I thought it hardly worth while referring to them. I quite realize that there are many of our raw materials which are not suited for certain classes of work, and naturally I intended this to apply only where it could properly apply, to those raw materials which can be used.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think perhaps the hon, gentleman did not hear me read item 607a, which contains this proviso:
Provided, that the governor in council may, when satisfied that the leather specified in this item is being produced in Canada in quantity and quality sufficient for Canadian requirements by order in council direct that this tariff item be repealed.
That is the amended item, and that meets the very suggestion which, despite what my hon. friend from Weyburn says, I think is a sound one, that we should encourage the production within this country, at the earliest possible moment, of those which enter into the production of the finished article with which we are dealing.

The system of granting
rebates of duty which has grown up in this country during the last few years has been one of the curses of the system of protection.
One of the curses?

Yes; there may be others as well, but if this could be corrected-and I understand from the Prime Minister he is on the way to correcting it-I certainly will approve of what he is trying to do. I do not
believe in the rebate system. I believe in protection, and I think if we can do away with the rebate proposition we will accomplish something worth while.

the stoiy of those who declined to listen. There would be no flood, they said; and for a long time there was no flood. Then the deluge came and that was the end of them*

This is the basket item-"all goods not enumerated." I do not not know who particularly would be interested in this item. Can the Prime Minister say where the requests came from?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should say there were no fewer than two score and ten applications, and if my memory does not deceive me, probably sixty. It was general throughout the country. The hon. gentleman will realize why the applications were made. This is an item of such importance that under present economic conditions if it were left at the rates at present provided the effect might be disastrous with respect to many matters that fall within it. In order to maintain some measure of uniformity between other items and this one the rates have been raised as indicated, from 174 per cent to 25 per cent. Coming specifically within the item are certain drugs and preparations on which an increase was sought, and there are a great many items of that kind.

The position is something like this. The manufacturer of a certain kind of drug finds that his product falls into the basket and he asks for an increase in the whole basket in order that he may obtain a higher rate for his particular line. And that happened with sixty other commodities. Requests were made for increases on sixty different articles and the Prime Minister responds by increasing everything in the basket.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman does violence to his own understanding when he speaks that way. He does not mean to put it in that form. The item in its present form has stood for about twenty years, and although there has been a very general change with respect to most other items, especially during the present stress and strain, this item has remained without a change during all that period. It is therefore out of line with the other tariff items. My hon. friend will agree that, if we are to apply to items that have been enumerated the general principles to which I have alluded in the course of the discussion, the basket item, to be in line with the others, should be increased at least from 174 per cent to 25 per cent. Of the importations under this item, $1,500,000 came from Great Britain and $18,250,000 from the United States. The total is much greater, but those are the largest items. The old rate was 15 per cent, 174 per cent and 174 per cent. It is not usual that the intermediate and general tariffs should be the same, but twenty years ago there was practically no protection
Ways and Means-Drawbacks

such as that to which I alluded during the discussion this afternoon, and so this item has been increased to be brought in line with the other items of the tariff. Although my hon. friend may disagree with the general principle of our tariff legislation, I think he will agree that there is in this increase a general recognition of the necessity of maintaining some relative proportion between the various items which go to make up the tariff as a whole.

Last year when the producers of strawberries could not dispose of their crop, the government of British Columbia advanced the price of the sugar necessary to process these strawberries in cold storage. Has the minister considered sugar used for this purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This item would not cover that. I would like to pay a tribute to the hon. gentleman's resourcefulness as this is the first time the suggestion has been offered.
The government of British Columbia advanced the price of the sugar to the growers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will take up this matter with the departmental officials between now and to-morrow.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: subtopic

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should like to table a copy of the
trade agreement between Canada and Australia, in order that it may be printed in the votes and proceedings of to-morrow.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I was going to
ask my right hon. friend whether it would be possible to give us the Australian rates,- preferential, intermediate and general, opposite the items which appear in the schedule of the agreement. Although the schedule states that the British preferential rate, for example, is the rate that will govern, we do not know what the British preferential rate in Australia is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We are being advised
daily of changes in the Australian tariff rates. One came in on Friday. Their tariff is engaging their attention at present, but to the extent to which that information may be available, my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) tells me that it will be given.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It has been
pointed out to me that article II, section 1, paragraph (b) reads:
To all other goods the produce or manufacture of Canada, when imported into Australia, the benefits of the British preferential tariff.
What are the items that would be included under that section?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: All the items that are not set forth in the schedule.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Could the
minister give us a list of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There are, I think, some
416 items. I shall endeavour to-morrow to give what the right hon. gentleman asks for but it may not be strictly accurate because the Australian parliament is now engaged in a revision of its tariff.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We shall be
satisfied with whatever reservations the minister wishes to make so long as we get such information as may be available.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We shall do the best we
can.
On motion of Mr. Bennett the house adjourned at 10.58 p.m
Tuesday, July 14, 1931.
